p: Sam Okafor, a former Air Force crew chief who'd never run a project, took over the Halcyon in January after the first manager, Bea Kowal, walked out, and agency director Imogen Hale signed his two page charter, which names the launch window as the one thing nobody can move.
His first forecast gave about one in five odds of launching on February 18, 2063, and on his daughter Ada's count of the station's air, 952 days, the ship arrives seventeen days too late.
He told Ada the truth about the odds in his first log about the job.

Then, past midnight, he found Bea's folder named DO NOT CLOSE, holding AR 2207: in a 2059 test the departure stage's main oxidizer valve twitched for 40 milliseconds, two retests were clean, and the report was downgraded and closed as unexplained, with Bea's signature on it.
Her note on the folder says somebody has to open it again, and going into this chapter the question is whether that's Sam.
Wendell Price. The test conductor at the stand, sixty nine.
Quinn Abernathy. The scheduler, fast becoming Sam's right hand.
Imogen Hale. Director of the Ares Relief Authority, which owns the mission and pays for it.
Frances Odum. Chair of Families of Ares, the colonists' relatives.

Friday, February 4, 2061. 5:25 AM. Sam hadn't slept. Around three he'd stopped pretending and printed AR 2207 on the printer in Ada's room, the one with the cartoon tomato sticker she'd stuck on the lid when she was eleven. At a quarter to five he'd put his boots on and driven east on I-70 in the dark, with the printout face up on the passenger seat, as if it wanted to see where they were going.

The test stand was two miles past the high bay on a gravel road the county had stopped plowing in 2050. In the dark it was a tower of white lights standing in the middle of nothing, with the departure stage bolted into it, frost blankets over its lower half like somebody had tucked it in. The wind came across the prairie with nothing to stop it between here and Kansas and leaned on the truck hard enough that he felt it in the wheel. Wendell Price's pickup was already in the lot. It was always already in the lot.

Wendell was in the blockhouse with his boots up on a cable tray and the lid of a thermos balanced on his knee, watching four screens that showed the stage from four sides. He didn't turn around. You found Bea's folder.
Nobody drives out here at five in the morning to look at a building. He took his boots off the tray. She was going to ask me about it. December. She had it on a sticky note.
Sam thought of the note on the bezel of Bea's monitor, square capitals. ASK W ABOUT STAND. He'd read it every morning for four weeks and taken it for a reminder about a seal.

No. She ran out of December. He pointed at the third screen, at a gray cylinder about the size of a beer keg low on the stage, in a nest of lines, wrapped in its own blanket. That's her. Main oxidizer isolation valve. August of '59, she twitched on cycle three. Forty milliseconds. We cycled her twice more that afternoon and she was perfect both times.
Sam had the report open on his phone. The report says stand noise.
Stand had noise that summer. Ground fault on the instrumentation bus, June till we found it in September. Three channels spiking. I wrote it up.

Wendell looked at him for the first time. I said the stand had noise. Nobody asked me if that valve did. They asked if the stand had noise that summer, and I said yes, because it did. He picked up the thermos lid, found it empty, and set it down again. Pull the file. Look at the pressure channel downstream of her. Then come back out here and ask me the right question.

By 8:30 the file was on the big screen in the program room, and Quinn had it plotted. She'd come in at seven without being asked, because she'd seen his truck in the lot at six, which he'd forgotten she would. Two lines on the plot mattered. One was the sensor that said where the valve's poppet sat. The other was a pressure gauge just downstream of it, on a different rack.

Stand 2 data, the valve's acceptance test, Monday, August 18, 2059, cycle 3 of 5. The close command goes out at zero. At 208 milliseconds both sensors say closed. Six milliseconds later the position sensor says the poppet has lifted four tenths of a millimeter off its seat, while the limit switch still says closed. They disagree for 40 milliseconds, then agree again. Channel 31, a pressure gauge just downstream on Rack B, ripples by 3.1 psi inside that same window. The position sensor is on Rack A. Both racks share instrumentation ground bus 2.

Quinn put her finger on the screen, on the little hump in channel 31. That's on a different rack. If it's noise, it's noise that happened on two racks at once and knew exactly when to start. She read the last line again. Same ground bus, though. She sat back. So it's the valve coming off its seat and letting a little oxygen past, or it's the ground fault, and this file can't tell you which. Two retests, same afternoon, same stand, same crew, same ground fault. She had both hands flat on the table.
At 8:55 Hana Iwasaki came in early for the nine o'clock with her laptop under her arm, saw the plot on the wall, and stopped a step inside the door.

That's closed, she said. She said it to the plot. She didn't look at Sam. She set her laptop down on the table, picked it back up, said she'd be at the stand, and left, and the door took its time closing behind her on the pneumatic arm.
She was in the room when it closed, Quinn said quietly. Everybody was.

Sam looked at the forty milliseconds for a long time after Quinn went to get coffee. He knew what this was. A form somebody had closed with a doubt still behind it. He knew how that felt from the inside, because once, in Arizona, in 2041, he'd been the one holding the pen, with an indication on a jet that came and went and an hour he didn't have. He didn't think about that, as a rule. The rule had held for nineteen years. It wasn't holding this morning.

At 9:14 Garrett's email came in. Sam. Readiness Board wants the integrated plan for its March 21 session. All of it. Let's talk Monday. G. Over the high bay doors the countdown clock said 744. Sam folded the printout of AR 2207 in half and put it in his desk drawer. Then he took it back out and laid it flat on top of the desk, where he'd have to look at it.
Sam's got a wall of other people's plans in front of him. So did I on the Petrel, with a red marker.

385 days before launch. oh six thirty, integrated timeline up on the wall, flow 3. eleven sheets, taped end to end. Wendell says the tape will outlast the program. oh seven hundred, every subsystem drew its own bars. prop. gnc. hab. crew. range. nobody's bars touch anybody else's. that's a lie. went down the wall with the red marker. oh eight forty, 41 places where the bars touch. nobody owns any of them. I do now. oh nine fifteen, drew the window at the right edge. two lines. Mori says it looks like a gate. oh nine sixteen, it is a gate. oh nine twenty, across the top: the gate is real. the bars in front of it are guesses. eleven hundred, administrator walked through. asked why the bars have fuzzy ends. told him because they do. fourteen hundred, scope review. what Petrel won't carry. Tate asked for her keyboard. 4 kg. denied. she said she'll hum. seventeen thirty, L minus 385. tape holding.

Monday, February 7. Garrett came down to the program room himself at 7:40, which he never did, with a coffee from the place in Bennett and a printout of the board clerk's email. The Independent Readiness Board would meet on March 21 and wanted, the clerk wrote, "the program's integrated project management plan." Someone had underlined integrated twice, and it hadn't been Garrett.

Quinn had pulled together everything that might count. The integrated master schedule, thirty one thousand lines. A risk management plan from 2059 describing a risk review board that had last met in the spring. A quality plan that lived at Aldergrove and referred to Tallgrass as "the customer." Rafa's release plan, which was a board in his team's tool covered in colored notes. The procurement terms, which were inside four contracts. The communication plan for the Breather work. Nothing joined any of them to any of the others. Nobody's name was on the whole thing, because there wasn't a whole thing.
It's a stack of documents and a board, she said. I don't think it's a plan. I think it's a pile.

Sam puts every lead's name on a one page table, with the section each one owns and the date it's due. Then he and Quinn spend two evenings on the part nobody owns, the joints. Where the risk plan's reviews feed the schedule. Where Aldergrove's quality plan has to hand its test data to Wendell. Where Rafa's release plan lands on the hardware's red dates. They find thirty six places where two documents assume different things. Hana reads the list and says, Thirty six. I'd have bet forty. It's the first joke she's made anywhere near him in a week, and she still doesn't quite look at him while she makes it.

The integrated plan joins the subsidiary plans and the baselines into one document that says how the project gets run, watched, and closed. The leads own their parts. You own the whole, and the seams most of all, because a gap between two good plans is still a gap. Then you keep it current.

Tuesday, February 8. Hana had missed Monday's leads meeting with a calendar note that said stand. She'd missed Tuesday's standup with a note that said stand. Wendell, asked, said she'd spent both days out there running leak checks that didn't need her.
Sam had the stand file on his laptop and the pressure trace printed and folded in his jacket. He had the feeling, which he didn't like, that the whole building knew what was in his jacket.

Rafa caught him in the hall by the vending machines. Whatever it is, she's been carrying it since before you got here, he said, which was more than Rafa usually said about anyone on the hardware side. Just so you know.

He finds her at dusk on the stand's upper deck, out of the wind behind the oxidizer tank, with her hood up and her hands in her sleeves. He gives her the printout. She holds it flat against the tank so it won't blow away. He asks what that August was like, and then he shuts up. She talks for a long time about the ground fault, three channels spiking for months, her and Wendell chasing it through every connector on two racks with flashlights in their teeth. I believed it was noise. I still mostly believe it. A gust takes the end of the sentence, and she waits for it to pass. Mostly is a terrible word for a valve. Below them a pronghorn crosses the access road, stops, and goes on. Sam asks if there's anything she wants him to know before he decides. If you open it, don't do it to me in a meeting. He tells her he won't. She looks at him then, for about a second, and hands the trace back folded smaller than he gave it to her.

Engaging a stakeholder starts with listening. Take the evidence to the person first, privately, and try to understand what they saw and why they decided what they did. Code 3.2.3 asks you to actively listen to other points of view, seeking to understand them, and 3.2.7 asks you, ideally, to go directly to the person you disagree with. The trust you build now is what lets the formal process work later.

Thursday, February 10. Sam had spent two days learning the anomaly process the way he'd once learned a new jet's tech orders, from the front. Anyone could open an anomaly report. Only a disposition could close one: explained and fixed, explained and accepted, or, when nobody could find a cause and the thing didn't happen again, UNR. Unexplained, not repeatable. Reopening a closed report took the program manager's signature and nothing else.

Nothing else on paper. Off paper, AR 2207 had been closed for seventeen months, and every test on the departure stage since had been built on the valve being fine. Quinn ran the numbers at lunch. A real investigation, if it came to a new test campaign, could cost the stand three to eight weeks, and the stand was already on the critical path.
At 4:30 Hana sent him one line. Whatever you decide, I'll run it straight.

The form was on his screen with the cursor blinking in the box that said REASON FOR REOPENING. It was 5:15, the light outside was going orange over the prairie, and the clock over the high bay doors said 738.

He types the reason in one sentence. Closure rationale not supported by independent evidence; failure mode is criticality 1 by consequence. He signs it. Then he calls Hana before the system can email her, so she hears it from him, and tells her the investigation is hers to run, with Wendell. Okay, she says. Then, after a while, Thank you for calling first. At 5:40 he sends the board's clerk a one paragraph notice. At 5:52 Garrett calls. Sam lets it ring, opens the trace, and calls him back at six and walks him through it. Garrett listens to the whole thing. That's three to eight weeks. Maybe. You know what you're doing to me. Yes. Garrett hangs up without saying goodbye, which with Garrett isn't the worst thing that can happen.

A closed report with a doubt behind it is an unmanaged risk with a signature on it. Reopening it puts it back where the process can see it, own it, and work it. Give it to the people who know the hardware, tell the person who made the original call before anyone else, and tell governance. Identify the risk honestly, then let the process do its job.

Monday, February 14. Valentine's Day, which Sam remembered at 6:50 AM because the grocery store in Bennett had a rack of red balloons by the door and he stood looking at it longer than a man buying coffee should. Grace had liked the cheap ones, the kind that went soft by Wednesday.

By eight he was in the program room for the argument the integrated plan had turned up. Bea's work breakdown structure covered the hardware down to the fasteners: three modules, the Breather, ground support, the launch campaign, a little over four hundred work packages. For flight software it had one box labeled SOFTWARE, and under it, in Bea's capitals, ASK RAFA.

Rafa had come ready. My scope is a backlog. Eleven hundred items, ranked. The top fifty are ready to build. The bottom four hundred are guesses with titles. If you make me turn that into work packages with dates, I'll do it, and it'll be fiction by the next demo.
Hana didn't look up from her laptop. And if the valve commands are a guess with a title, I requalify. Again.

Quinn redraws the software box. Under it go the release milestones, tied to the hardware's red dates, and one line that points to Rafa's backlog as the element's content. Any backlog item that needs hardware has to name the WBS element it touches. Rafa reads it twice. So my whole team is one box. One box with a door in it. Does the door lock? On the red dates. Rafa thinks about it and says that's fair, which is the first time anyone in the room has heard him use the word.

In a hybrid project the WBS can hold the whole scope while part of it stays adaptive. Decompose the hardware into work packages you can estimate and baseline. Put the software in as an element whose content is the ranked backlog, and tie its releases to the integration dates. One scope, two ways of managing it, and a seam somebody owns.

Wednesday, February 16. The scope statement was eleven pages, and the first ten were easy, because they said what the ship would do. Page eleven was the exclusions, and it was blank except for a sticky note Bea had left on the draft. DO THIS PART LAST. EVERYONE WILL HATE IT.
Quinn had pulled the items together from the 2058 requirements, the mass budget, and every meeting where somebody had asked for something and been told no. The biggest one was a single paragraph.

HALCYON PROJECT SCOPE STATEMENT DRAFT 3 SECTION 11, EXCLUSIONS. 11.1 Earth return. Halcyon carries no ascent vehicle and no return propellant. It will not bring any colonist, or its own crew, back to Earth. The crew of four remains at Ares Station until a return opportunity in a later window. 11.2 Station expansion beyond the Breather, spare stacks, seed stock, and medical cargo. 11.3 A second lander. 11.4 Personal cargo above 2 kg per colonist.
Hale had read the draft over the weekend. Her note beside 11.1 was in blue ink: Do we have to say this? Garrett's, under hers: Call it "future capability." Investors like future.
Commander Yusra Haddad had four kids in Aurora. She'd read 11.1 too. She hadn't written anything.

He takes Hale the mass budget and the reason in one sentence: the window gives them exactly enough lift for the Breather and the people to install it, and not one ascent vehicle more. If I sign that, I'm on record saying we're leaving four people on Mars. You're on record either way, ma'am. This way it's in your words. She signs it Friday. Yusra reads it in the gym at the training center in Aurora, still sweaty, feet up on a weight bench, and then reads it again. I signed up for one way in 2059. I'd like my husband to hear it from you before he reads it. On Saturday Sam sits at the Haddads' kitchen table for an hour. Four kids are being quiet on purpose in the next room, badly, and the youngest keeps coming in for water.

Define the scope, including what it won't do, and get agreement from the stakeholders it affects most. Plain words and a reason make the boundary something people can accept, or argue with honestly. Exclusions are where projects come apart later, so settle them on paper now.

Friday, February 18, 2061. Two years to the day. Somebody on second shift had taped a paper party hat to the countdown clock over the doors, a gold one, a little crushed, and under it the clock said 730.

The Breather was the reason for the ship and the least broken down thing in it. Bea's WBS had one element for it, BREATHER (OXYGEN PLANT), with four boxes underneath: stacks, water, power, controls. The electrochemistry team was eleven people in a lab at the far end of the high bay where the air smelled like a swimming pool. Their lead, Owen Talbot, a soft spoken man with a beard he kept trimming shorter as the winter went on, had brought his own breakdown, and it was organized by who sat where.
These are my four groups, he said. That's the work.

Quinn drew his four boxes on the whiteboard. Under them she sketched the lander, and off to the right the station, and ran a line from one to the other. Then she stood there with the cap of the marker in her teeth and didn't say what the line was for.

Two afternoons, most of the whiteboard, and a second box of markers. Plant hardware, yes, and also everything that has to exist before the plant can breathe for anybody: the install kit, the procedures, training for the station's engineers, a cutover from the old plant with no gap in it, the spares, and the test that proves the whole thing works at Mars pressure. When they add the pieces back up, Quinn finds what nobody owned. The last four hundred meters, from the lander to the plant room, across the regolith, at sixty below. I thought the station did that. The station thought we did. They write a WBS dictionary entry for every package, and Owen trims his beard again that weekend, which Quinn says is a good sign.

Decompose the scope by deliverable, with the people who'll do the work, down to work packages small enough to estimate and own. Then apply the 100 percent rule: the children have to add up to all of the parent and nothing outside it. That check is how you find the work that falls between teams.

Tuesday, February 22. Quinn had printed the risk register, because she said she couldn't think about it on a screen. Four hundred and twelve lines in eight point type, stapled at the corner, sorted by score the way it had always been sorted, highest first.
It took Sam twenty minutes to find the valve. It was on page nine.

Risk register, line 371 of 412. Risk 388: the departure stage valve's position indication anomaly, from AR 2207. Likelihood 1, rare. Impact 3, crit 2. Score 3. Owner, propulsion. Response, accept. Status, closed with the AR.
AR 2207 had been open again for twelve days. Its line in the register still said closed.
Directly above it, at line 370, was the risk that the program's coffee service contract would lapse. Score 4.

Sam read the top twenty. Most of them were written the way registers get written by tired people. Schedule pressure on stage integration. Thermal margin concerns. Nothing in any of them said what would happen to whom. He'd spent nine years on a flight line where the forms used plain words because the people reading them were nineteen and exhausted, and the plain words were part of what kept the nineteen year olds alive.

Quinn and Sam spend the afternoon rewriting the top forty lines in one form, his flight line form: if this happens, then this, and this is who gets hurt. The valve line becomes If the main oxidizer isolation valve fails to close on command at departure burn cutoff, the stage overburns, and the crew of four and the colony's air end up on a trajectory that doesn't reach Mars. Severity: crit 1. Likelihood: unknown, written as unknown. Owner: Hana. Trigger: any position disagreement, on any cycle, anywhere. Sorted by severity first, it's on page one. Wendell reads the new top forty standing at Quinn's desk and doesn't say anything for a while. Then he says, That's the first one of these I ever read all the way through.

Identify and analyze risks honestly, and keep the two axes apart: impact comes from the consequence, likelihood from the evidence. If the likelihood is unknown, write unknown. Every risk needs an owner, a response, and a trigger, and the register has to be written so a tired person can read it and know what's at stake.

Thursday, February 24. Every requirement that touched the program lived in a compliance matrix, nine thousand rows, kept by an ARA mission assurance office in Denver that Sam had met exactly once. Quinn had spent two nights in it. After the register she'd wanted to know one thing: whether AR 2207 was the only report on Halcyon that had ever been downgraded.

It wasn't. There were four. All four had started at criticality 1 and been revised to criticality 2 with a rationale about test conditions, and each of them had closed in the month before a schedule review. Because each one was crit 2 on the day it closed, Flight Rule 2.36 showed against all four as not applicable.
AR 2207 was open again. The other three weren't. They were small things on the departure stage and the habitat: a heater, a pressure switch, a hatch latch.
None of them broke the rule, Quinn said. That's what I can't stop looking at. Nobody broke it. They went around it the same way four times.

Quinn pulls every downgrade back to 2058. There are four, and only these four. Sam sends the board a two page memo that names the reports, the dates, the reviews they came before, and what each rationale rested on. It names no people. At the bottom it proposes one control: no crit 1 report on Halcyon gets downgraded without the board's written concurrence. The clerk logs it as Question sixty one oh four for the March session. The next morning the clerk's acknowledgment comes back with the memo stamped and numbered, and in the margin, beside the stamp, a small tick in green ink. Docketed. R.C. Sam looks at the two letters for a while before he files it.

Confirm the compliance requirements, look for threats to them, and measure how far the project really complies. A workaround used four times is a threat to compliance even when every instance met the letter of the rule. Report it to the governance that owns the rule and propose a control that closes the gap. Code 2.3.1 asks you to uphold the rules that govern your work, and that includes what they're for.

Monday, February 28. 5:40 AM. One way light time this morning was six minutes and twenty eight seconds, the shortest it had been since Ada landed. In April it would bottom out a little over five, and Quinn had put a note on the program calendar that said CLOSEST, with no explanation, as if everyone would know what it meant. Everyone did.

A log from Ada Okafor, Ares Station. Sol 3565. One way, 6 minutes 28 seconds. Margin, 911 days. Hi, Dad. I have tomatoes. Nine of them, on the Bay C vines, red. Actually red. You don't know what red does to a person who's looked at orange dirt for two years. I'm cutting one into twelve pieces for the shift tonight, and Dr. Lindgren gets a piece, because she finally stopped asking about the basil. Your last log. I watched it twice, like always. You look tired in that kitchen light. It's the bulb over the table, Dad. It's been dying since I was in high school. Change the bulb. Okay. Real stuff. We had our first ration cut four sols ago. Hollis calls it a consumption adjustment. Calories down a tenth, three gym sessions a week instead of six, and the rec module goes dark at 2100 so we'll sleep more and breathe less. It's very scientific. It's also everybody hungry and in bed early, like a summer camp nobody signed up for. Hollis's report says it buys fifteen days. I ran it off the plant log, same as before. I get eight. So my number's nine hundred eleven by the time you hear this. I know what you're doing right now. You're doing subtraction on the back of something. One more thing, then tomatoes again. Teodor in the machine shop worked for a valve company in Pueblo before he came out. He says there's a woman there who's been arguing about one valve for twenty six years, and everybody at the company calls her the valve lady. He also says, and I'm only telling you what's going around the galley, that a valve on your ship did something weird in a test a couple of years ago and somebody closed the paperwork. Everybody here's heard it by now. Nobody here can check it. That's the bad part, up here. You hear a thing and there's nothing to do with it except hear it again at dinner. Have you met the valve lady? If she's real, I want to know what she's been arguing about. Remember the chore chart? Color coded, laminated, with a legend. I was nine. Mom said you'd made a Gantt chart for a fourth grader, and you said it was a responsibility matrix, and she laughed so hard she had to sit down on the stairs. I'm running the hydroponics expansion off a chart now. It's laminated. I hate that you were right. Love you. Nine hundred eleven. Ada out.

He got the gas bill out from under the fruit bowl. Under minus seventeen he wrote her new number and ran it against the arrival date. Minus nine. Eight days better, because two hundred and twelve people were going to bed hungry at nine o'clock. Hollis's report, the one the ARA posted every Monday, would still say fifty eight to spare.
Then the valve. There was an old report. Eighteen days ago he'd reopened it. That was the true answer, and it was the only one he could give her yet, and it wasn't the whole of what she was asking.

At 9:20 Frances Odum, who chaired Families of Ares, called his cell. She didn't say hello. Malik's message came in this morning. He says they're on rations and in bed by nine, and Hollis calls it an adjustment. A breath. Families of Ares has a call Thursday. Two hundred people. Most of them have one question. They've heard the ship won't bring anybody home, and they want to know if it's true. Some of them have sick kids up there, Mr. Okafor. They want a seat.

Thursday he sits in front of a laptop in the program room with two hundred faces on the screen and Frances in the corner tile. He says it the way it's written: nobody comes home on Halcyon. He says why, with the mass budget, in one sentence. Then he stops talking and asks what they need. It takes forty minutes. Most of them don't need a seat they know isn't there. They need the program's real forecast every month, with the odds. They need somebody at the program who answers email. They need to know which medicines are in the cargo. He writes it all down and commits to all three that week, with the email as his own job. At the end Frances says, That's the first time anybody from Tallgrass has told us something we didn't want to hear. She doesn't say thank you. She doesn't hang up first, either.

Managing expectations starts with finding out what they are. Then you align what the project will deliver with them, out loud, bad news included. Here the customers are the colonists and their families. Telling them what's excluded and asking what they need turns a fight over a seat into a list you can do something about.
Thursday, March 3. Hale came out to Watkins at noon with Gwen Talley, her chief of staff, and a printout, and this time she sat down.

ARA OFFICE OF THE DIRECTOR REQUEST. Add an external camera to the habitat module to carry the departure burn and Mars arrival live. Countdown to Ares has offered to stream both free to its audience (40 million). Partners strongly in favor. Needed for the May partner meeting: confirmation that it's in the baseline.
Forty million people watching that ship leave, she said. Do you know what that does to a budget vote?

Rafa, who'd been asked to sit in, said the ship already had six navigation cameras, and he could probably stream two of them with a software change and no new hardware. Hana said probably was doing a lot of work in that sentence, since the navigation cameras fed guidance. Quinn wrote on her pad and turned it so Sam could read it. HAB MASS MARGIN 410 KG. EACH KG ON HAB COSTS ABOUT 2 KG OF PROPELLANT.

The change process written into the plan in February named a change board: Sam, the ARA's mission assurance lead, and Hale's deputy, with anything over a threshold going up to Hale. Hale was the sponsor. Today she was also the person asking.

Sam tells Hale it'll be a change request by Friday and a decision in two weeks, with both options on it, and that she'll hear the answer before the partners do. She doesn't love the two weeks. The analysis turns up more than anybody expected. The hardware camera costs 31 kilos, about 62 of propellant, and a thermal rerun. Rafa's option costs no mass, but it needs a bus load test and a guidance requalification, which Hana insists on and Rafa, to his credit, agrees to. The change board approves Rafa's option, conditional on the test, and writes down why. Quinn sends Hale a one page status that afternoon. Hale reads it and says, You made me wait two weeks for a yes. For a yes you won't have to take back, ma'am.

Every change, from anyone, takes the same path: write it down, analyze its impact on scope, schedule, cost, quality, and risk, decide it at the right level, update the plan, and tell the requester where it stands. A sponsor asking doesn't change the process. It makes doing the process well matter more.

Wednesday, March 9. 711 on the clock. Quinn's schedule was ready to baseline, which meant it was ready to become the thing every slip would be measured against for two years, which meant everybody wanted to change it today.

It had come up from the bottom: the leads' own estimates from January, the work packages from February, the Breather breakdown, Rafa's release milestones. AR 2207's investigation was in it too, Hana's estimate, three to eight weeks of stand time, sitting on the critical path like a rock in a creek. On the leads' own numbers, February 18 was still possible and still not likely.

Garrett had his own version. Someone in finance had moved the Breather's acceptance test two weeks earlier, into a week the stand looked free. Sam looked at the week. It was the week Wendell had blocked for the stand's seal change, which was written in Wendell's pocket notebook and nowhere else.
Baseline mine, Garrett said. It's got float on the 18th. Investors can read float.

Quinn has the leads sign their sections one at a time at her cube, so nobody signs in a crowd. Rafa signs the release milestones and asks for the backlog itself to stay unbaselined, which is the whole point, and Quinn tells him so, and he looks pleased anyway. Hana signs, then asks to see the stand calendar one more time and reads it with her finger. Hale approves the baseline on the 11th with one line: Baselined on the team's estimates. Confidence reported monthly. Garrett wants the float explained to him in person. Halfway down the page he gets to the seal change and stops. Who knew about that? Wendell. Only Wendell? Until about ten this morning. Garrett takes his reading glasses off and taps them on the page twice, which is a thing Sam has never seen him do.

Prepare the schedule to fit the approach: hardware in detail, software at the level of releases tied to integration dates, the backlog left free to change. Build it from the estimates of the people doing the work, coordinate it with operations, then baseline it through governance. The baseline should measure the plan you actually have.

Monday, March 21. The Independent Readiness Board met in a federal building downtown, in a room with good chairs, bad coffee, and a seal on the wall nobody looked at. Seven members sat at a curved table. Ruth was at the end, with the green pen.
The program's integrated plan was due to the board by noon. It was finished. Sam had read every section of it, and he knew which parts he believed.
AR 2207 was in it, open, with Hana's investigation on the critical path.

What bothered him most wasn't the valve. Every date in the plan sat on one assumption, the ARA's oxygen margin model. On that model, arrival on September 6, 2063 left fifty eight days to spare. On the lower number Sam had seen, the one under his fruit bowl, the ship arrived nine days late. Nobody at the agency had yet said on the record which number was right.
Quinn had the cover memo open on her laptop. What do you want it to say?

The page has five lines. The first says the whole plan depends on the ARA's oxygen margin model, that station engineering data the program has seen runs about two months lower, and that on the lower number the plan arrives nine days late. The board reads it during the morning break. When the session resumes, Ruth Calder, the retired flight director, asks the only question she asks all day. Mr. Okafor. On the lower number, does your plan get air there in time? No, ma'am. Not as it stands. The room goes quiet the way rooms do when somebody has said the thing. The chair asks the ARA's representative when the agency will verify its model. The representative says soon. The chair says May, and writes it down, and so does everybody else at the table.

Assess the consolidated plan for dependencies, gaps, and continued business value, and say what you found. The value here is air at Ares in time. If the plan can't show that on every credible number, the board needs to know in the first paragraph. Name the critical information the plan rests on, and ask for it to be verified.

Friday, March 25. Ruth's second page came in the mail, in a long envelope addressed in green ink with a Golden postmark and no return address. Sam didn't open it in the driveway. He set it on the kitchen table against the fruit bowl, made dinner, ate it standing at the counter, and kept an eye on the envelope the whole time, like a dog that might bolt.

AR 2207 had been open for six weeks. Hana's team had pulled every stand record from the summer of 2059, and Wendell had found the ground bus drawings in a flat file nobody had opened since the fault was fixed. Nothing they'd found yet said noise, and nothing said valve. Hana had started looking at him in meetings again. Not every time.
At eight he sat down with the tablet against the fruit bowl to answer the last thing in Ada's log. He'd answered the tomatoes weeks ago. He'd left the valve for last.

There's an old report on a valve. It's real. I reopened it. That's all I can tell you about it right now, and it's true, and when there's more I'll tell you more. He didn't do the voice. He watched it back once to make sure.
I haven't met the valve lady. If she's real, I'll find her. That part he meant all the way down.
It had been a good seven weeks, as these things went. He didn't trust the thought. It had the same shape as a thought he'd had once in Arizona, on a Thursday, with a pen in his hand.

He opened Ruth's envelope at 9:40. Page two was inside, the one about the timeline on the wall. Behind it was a photocopy folded into eighths and soft at the creases. He unfolded it on the table, pushing the fruit bowl back to make room.

It was the timeline. Eleven sheets shrunk onto one, so the bars were thin as thread. The red circles where the bars touched had gone gray in the copy. At the right edge, two vertical lines: the gate. Across the top, in Ruth's 2034 capitals, THE GATE IS REAL. THE BARS IN FRONT OF IT ARE GUESSES.
He found the propulsion row with his finger. Near the left, early in the flow, a short bar labeled ISOL VLV ACCEPT. In the margin beside it, in green ink, somebody had written a part number.
PETREL INTEGRATED TIMELINE MAY 2034 PROPULSION ROW (COPY). ISOL VLV ACCEPT. MARGIN, GREEN INK: 7740-112

He didn't need to check it. He checked it anyway. The printout of AR 2207 from that first night was in the drawer by the phone charger, under Grace's reading glasses, where he'd put it the night he brought it home from his desk in February, without exactly deciding to. He unfolded it next to the timeline. ALDERGROVE FLUID SYSTEMS PART NUMBER 7740-112, REV F.
Same supplier. Same number. Two valves, twenty five years apart.

The rest of the copy had faded the way photocopies of old pages fade, everything a little gray. The part number hadn't. It was the exact green of the pen in Ruth's cardigan pocket, and it sat on top of the gray the way new ink does.

He sat with the two pages side by side until the furnace came on and went off again. Then he got the gas bill out from under the fruit bowl, turned it over, and under minus nine he wrote 7740-112. He didn't know yet what it meant. He knew who did.
